[[File:Hatiora salicornioides.jpg|thumb]]
'''''Hatiora salicornoides''''', also spelt '''''Hatiora salicornioides''''', the '''bottle cactus''', '''dancing-bones''', '''drunkard's-dream''',<ref name = GRIN/> or '''spice cactus''',<ref name=DT/> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[cactus]] family. A member of the tribe [[Rhipsalideae]], it often grows as an [[epiphyte]], natively in eastern [[Brazil]] and ornamentally elsewhere.

==Description==
''Hatiora salicornoides'' grows to about {{cvt|1|m|ft|0}} tall with an erect to pendent growth habit. Its stems are composed of segments {{cvt|1.5|–|5|cm|in|1}} long. Each segment is shaped like a club or bottle, with the narrower end at the base. The stems branch from the end of a segment, with up to six branches forming a whorl. The yellow to orange flowers are borne at the ends of younger stem segments, and are {{cvt|1|–|2|cm|in|1}} long and about the same across when open. Translucent white berries follow the flowers.<ref name=Ande01p377/>

==Taxonomy==
The species was first described by [[Adrian Hardy Haworth|Adrian H. Haworth]] in 1819, as ''Rhipsalis salicornoides''. Haworth spelled the specific epithet as ''salicornoides''; subsequent authors corrected the spelling to ''salicornioides'', regarding the original as an orthographic error.<ref name=BartTayl95/> The [[International Plant Names Index]] later deemed the specific epithet incorrectable to ''salicornioides'' as is it derived from a noun and a suffix rather than two Greek or Latin words.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rhipsalis salicornoides {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/312536-2 |access-date=2023-02-24 |website=www.ipni.org}}</ref> The epithet means "similar to ''[[Salicornia]]''". The species was placed under the genus ''Hatiora'' in 1915, after previously belonging to the “lost” (and ultimately, abandoned) genus of ''Hariota''.<ref name=POWO_118071-2/> [[Molecular phylogenetics|Molecular phylogenetic]] studies have confirmed its placement in the correct genus, and also in the tribe [[Rhipsalideae]], showing a close relation to ''[[Hatiora cylindrica|H. cylindrica]]'' (which has been considered synonymous with ''H. salicornoides'', as a cultivar/form or variety). ''H. salicornoides'' is highly variable, as many succulent plants can be, and may possibly include other distinct species.<ref name=CalvZappForeLohm11/><ref name=KoroBorsQuanTayl11/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Hatiora salicornoides'' is found along the coast (and slightly inland) of the [[Southeast Region, Brazil|Southeast Region of Brazil]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Observations • iNaturalist |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?nelat=-18.365682075278578&nelng=-34.900390525&place_id=any&subview=map&swlat=-27.43845741295175&swlng=-53.857174912500035&taxon_id=1453005 |access-date=26 May 2024 |website=[[iNaturalist]].org}}</ref> in states that are parallel to the [[Atlantic Ocean]]—although the plant is not typically found growing directly at sea level. Primarily, the species is known from the states of [[Bahia]], [[Espírito Santo]], [[Minas Gerais]], [[Rio de Janeiro (state)|Rio de Janeiro]], [[São Paulo (state)|São Paulo]] and [[Paraná (state)|Paraná]];<ref>{{Cite web |title=Observations • iNaturalist |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6878&subview=map&taxon_id=1453005 |access-date=25 May 2024 |website=[[iNaturalist]].org}}</ref> [[List of cities in Brazil by population|cities]] and [[Municipalities of Brazil|municipalities]] where it is known from include [[Belo Horizonte]], [[Curitiba]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Observations • iNaturalist |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=22960&subview=map&taxon_id=1453005 |access-date=26 May 2024 |website=[[iNaturalist]].org}}</ref> [[São José dos Pinhais]], and [[Tiradentes, Minas Gerais|Tiradentes]], among others; it may also be found in and around metro [[Rio de Janeiro]] and [[São Paulo]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Observations • iNaturalist |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=13334&subview=map&taxon_id=1453005 |access-date=26 May 2024 |website=[[iNaturalist]].org}}</ref> where it grows naturally among tall trees, parks and landscaping. Additionally, a number of large botanic gardens and national parks are situated close to—or directly inside of—the city limits of Río de Janeiro and São Paulo, such as [[Tijuca National Park]] and the [[Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden]], which help to provide a protected, natural habitat for these delicate [[Epiphyte|epiphytic]] cacti in the middle of two of the planet's most densely populated [[Megacity|megacities]].

The vast and fragile forested stretch of Southeastern Brazilian coastline, the Atlantic Forest [[ecoregion]] (or [[Atlantic Forest|''Mata Atlantico'']]), contains dense, and relatively still-intact, forest habitat burgeoning with [[Endemism|endemic]] flora and fauna, including a number of ''Hatiora'' species, among other jungle cacti. The region's rapid rate of plant growth, and high number of unique species, is attributed to a stable ambient humidity level and relatively consistent equatorial temperatures; in addition to the regular [[precipitation]] and [[Thunderstorm|thunderstorms]] the region receives, further humidity is gleaned by plants via [[fog]], [[marine layer]], and morning [[dew]]. The region is also flowing with numerous rivers and streams, along which dozens of epiphytic species may be seen growing on tree branches directly above the water, seemingly "intentionally", as to directly benefit from the ambient humidity and cooling breezes generated by the fast-flowing river. 

Within the Atlantic forests, and indeed much of Brazil's forested regions, the limbs of trees are often the most common places to find epiphytic cacti. ''Hatiora'' may be found growing in very high branches or closer to the [[forest floor]], or in peculiar and unexpected locations on any given tree. ''Hatiora'' grow and become established wherever they have sprouted (from dispersed seed) or taken root, [[Vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]], via a broken segment or cutting separating and landing on a new tree branch. Vegetative (asexual) reproduction is typically the fastest means by which epiphytic cacti species can spread and establish new habitats. The plants utilize trees, boulders, logs or other natural objects as permanent, fixed structures. Trees in Brazilian forests often become "communities" or symbiotic "networks" featuring a myriad of arboreal cacti growing with other epiphytic [[Family (taxonomy)|plant families]] and [[Genus|genera]], such as [[Araceae]], [[Bromeliaceae]], [[Fern|ferns]], [[Moss|mosses]], [[Orchid|Orchidaceae]], ''[[Peperomia]]'', ''[[Tradescantia]]'', and more.<ref name="POWO_118071-2" /> Every available space is used to its maximum potential in these productive rainforests, with the plant-laden trees giving an almost "dripping" appearance. With most of the aforementioned plant types, as well as ''Hatiora'', root nodes or [[Internode (botany)|internodes]]—part of the plant where each leaf connects with the next—will send out sticky-tipped aerial roots to anchor the plant in place, adhering to the textured tree bark. Once stability is achieved, the plants gradually grow and transform, moving slowly closer to the sunlight.<ref name="IUCN" />

In addition to thriving in moist forest, these diminutive cacti are also found growing on trees in the more open [[savanna]] habitats, rocky outcrops, humid canyons, as well as montane regions, at elevations of {{cvt|200|–|1750|m|ft|-1}}. It is seldom, if ever, found rooted into the ground, and nearly always found growing arboreally or as a [[lithophyte]].<ref name="IUCN" /> 

==Cultivation==
''Hatiora salicornoides'' is grown as an [[ornamental plant]]. It requires some humidity, and is not frost-tolerant. Light shade and a minimum average temperature of {{cvt|12|C|F|0}} are recommended. Given these conditions, it has been successfully cultivated outside in [[Phoenix, Arizona]]. In climates with lower winter temperatures, it is cultivated in [[greenhouse]]s or as a house plant. It is propagated by [[Cutting (plant)|stem cuttings]].<ref name=DT/><ref name=Ande99/>

In the UK ''Hatiora salicornoides'' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/33717/Hatiora-salicornioides/Details | title = ''Hatiorna salicornioides'' | website = www.rhs.org | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 19 July 2020}}</ref>
